home-is-hard.name: Run-down home
home-is-hard.line: My home is cramped, falling apart or too noisy.
home-is-hard.why: Names the problem the way Homeless and Eviction do, so the Home heading stops mixing problem and area labels, and keeps the three everyday things people actually complain about.

home-is-hard.name: Bad housing
home-is-hard.line: The place I live is in bad shape, and I can't fix it or move.
home-is-hard.why: Says what makes it a pain rather than a list of faults: the place is bad and the person is stuck with it.

cold-home.name: Cold home
cold-home.line: I can't afford to keep my home warm.
cold-home.why: A problem name that matches the heading, and 'keep my home warm' is how people say it; it also sets this apart from being behind on the power bill.

cold-home.name: Cold or hot
cold-home.line: I can't afford to keep my home warm in winter or cool in summer.
cold-home.why: Echoes the earlier name Cold or hot home and covers summer heat, which hits many people as hard as winter cold.

unsafe-near-me.name: Unsafe area
unsafe-near-me.line: I don't feel safe in my neighborhood.
unsafe-near-me.why: Says where the danger is, so nobody mixes it up with Safety at home on the People page, and the name becomes a problem like the rest of the heading.

getting-around.name: Can't get around
getting-around.line: I can't easily get to work, the store or the doctor.
getting-around.why: Names the places people actually miss, which makes the line concrete, and turns the name into a problem like the rest of the heading.

offline.name: Bad internet
offline.line: I can't get internet that's fast enough and that I can afford.
offline.why: Keeps the earlier wording's two causes, speed and price, and makes the name a problem so it fits the heading if it is ever shown.

pairs.distinction: Homeless is having no reliable place to stay now; Eviction is still having a home and fearing losing it.
pairs.reason: Someone sleeping on a friend's couch and someone behind on rent know at once which one they are living with.
Having no place to stay myself and seeing more neighbors without homes are the same pain seen from the personal and societal pages, so they stay two pains linked across pages.

pairs.distinction: Eviction is the fear of losing my home; High rent is paying too much for it, which many people manage without any risk of losing it.
pairs.reason: High rent can lead to eviction, but people paying too much and people about to lose their home would each look for their own pain.

pairs.distinction: Eviction is my own home at risk; Homelessness is seeing neighbors who already have none.
pairs.reason: One is a personal fear and the other is something seen in the community, and the personal match for Homelessness is Homeless, not Eviction.

pairs.distinction: Housing is the place being cramped, broken or noisy; High rent is what it costs.
pairs.reason: Plenty of people pay too much for a decent place, and plenty live somewhere run-down that is cheap, so the choice is easy.

pairs.distinction: Heating is not being able to pay to keep warm, even in a sound home; Housing is the place itself being cramped, broken or noisy.
pairs.reason: A drafty, broken home can be cold too, but someone who can't afford the heating bill would look for that pain by name.

pairs.distinction: Heating is one specific cost going without; Rising costs is everything getting more expensive than pay.
pairs.reason: Going cold at home needs its own fixes, like heating help and insulation, and people living it would look for it rather than a general cost complaint.

pairs.distinction: Heating is going without warmth to avoid the bill; Utility bills is being behind on the bills already, which can include water.
pairs.reason: Many people keep the heat off so they never fall behind, so the alternative line 'I can't afford to keep my home warm' makes the difference clear.

pairs.distinction: Internet is not being able to get online at a decent speed or price; Transport is not being able to get to places.
pairs.reason: Both can cut people off from work and services, but nobody would confuse a slow connection with having no ride.
Not feeling safe where I live and not feeling safe from crime are the same pain seen from the personal and societal pages, so they stay two pains linked across pages.

pairs.distinction: Safety is danger in the neighborhood; Safety at home is danger from someone in my own life.
pairs.reason: The two need very different help, and the alternative name Unsafe area keeps them from both reading as Safety.
Struggling to get where I need to go and living in a place built only for cars are the same pain seen from the personal and societal pages, so they stay two pains linked across pages.

loneliness.name: Loneliness
loneliness.line: Most days I don't talk to anyone who really knows me.
loneliness.why: Keeps the plain name and says what being alone looks like in a day, which also sets it apart from having no one to call or no one to go out with.

loneliness.name: Company
loneliness.line: I go whole days without a real conversation with anyone.
loneliness.why: An area-style name like the rest of the People heading, with a line someone could picture and recognize as their own week.

no-one-to-lean-on.name: Someone to call
no-one-to-lean-on.line: I have no one to call when I need help.
no-one-to-lean-on.why: "Support" is the name of It's own Support It flow, so a different name avoids confusion; the line already says it well.

no-one-to-lean-on.name: No backup
no-one-to-lean-on.line: When something goes wrong, there's no one I can lean on.
no-one-to-lean-on.why: Uses the ID's own words for the line and makes the moment of need concrete, with a short name that isn't It's Support flow.

new-here.name: New in town
new-here.line: I just moved here and don't know anyone yet.
new-here.why: Says the situation rather than the act of moving, which could also mean the stress of packing or paying for a move.

nobody-to-do-things-with.name: Plans
nobody-to-do-things-with.line: I'd go out more if I had someone to go with.
nobody-to-do-things-with.why: Keeps the original wish to go out, and says the missing piece is a companion rather than an invitation, which matches the ID.

drifted-apart.name: Old friends
drifted-apart.line: I've drifted apart from friends who used to matter a lot to me.
drifted-apart.why: "Friends" alone could sit over several pains on this heading; "old friends" and "drifted apart" name this one.

lost-faith-community.name: Faith community
lost-faith-community.line: I left my faith community and lost my people with it.
lost-faith-community.why: The ID names a faith community, and the current name "Belonging" is the same as another pain's name on this heading.

lost-faith-community.name: Lost community
lost-faith-community.line: I've lost the community I used to be part of.
lost-faith-community.why: Keeps the broader meaning (church, team, scene, hometown) but gives it a name that doesn't repeat the Belonging pain.

pairs.distinction: Fighting at home is conflict; not feeling safe with someone is fear of being hurt, and may need crisis resources first.
pairs.reason: Someone afraid for their safety needs to find that pain without wondering whether ordinary family fights are the same thing.

pairs.distinction: Struggling with a partner is a hard relationship; not feeling safe is about danger, and the person may not be a partner.
pairs.reason: Folding danger into relationship trouble would hide a sensitive pain inside an everyday one.

pairs.distinction: Loneliness is the overall feeling of being alone; the other is wanting company for going out.
pairs.reason: Someone can have close people and still have no one to go out with, so a person can choose between them, more easily if the loneliness line is made concrete.

pairs.distinction: Loneliness is day-to-day isolation; no one to lean on is having nobody to call in a crisis.
pairs.reason: Plenty of people with a busy social life have no one they'd call at 2am, and the fixes differ.

pairs.distinction: Belonging is about fitting into a group or place; loneliness is about missing people day to day.
pairs.reason: People often feel they don't fit in anywhere while still having a few friends, so the two read differently.

pairs.distinction: Belonging is never having found a place; the other is losing one you had.
pairs.reason: Losing a community you had is a grief of its own, but the two currently share the name Belonging, which the alternatives fix.

pairs.distinction: Dating is about finding a partner; intimacy is missing closeness, which people in relationships feel too.
pairs.reason: Someone married can miss closeness without wanting to date, so the two are easy to tell apart.

pairs.distinction: Relationship strain is conflict or difficulty with a partner; intimacy is missing closeness, with or without one.
pairs.reason: A calm relationship can lack closeness and a close one can be full of fights, so neither covers the other.

pairs.distinction: Dating is wanting a romantic partner; loneliness is missing people in general.
pairs.reason: Many people want a partner without feeling alone, and many feel alone without wanting to date.

pairs.distinction: New in town has a clear cause and its own fixes (meeting neighbors, local groups); loneliness can last for years with no move.
pairs.reason: Someone who just moved will recognize their situation right away, and the fixes for it are specific.

pairs.distinction: New in town is knowing nobody where you live; the other is lacking company for going out, even among people you know.
pairs.reason: Knowing nobody at all and knowing people who don't invite you are different situations.

pairs.distinction: This is losing a specific community you belonged to; loneliness is missing people in general.
pairs.reason: Leaving a church or other close community is a loss people name on its own.

pairs.distinction: Interests is about finding people who share a passion; the other is about having company at all.
pairs.reason: Someone with plenty of friends can still have no one who loves what they love.

pairs.distinction: Drifted apart is losing touch with particular friends; loneliness is the overall feeling of being alone.
pairs.reason: Missing old friends is specific enough to choose without thinking twice, and the fix is reaching back out.

pairs.distinction: Relationship is trouble with a partner; family is fighting among the people you live with, often parents, kids or siblings.
pairs.reason: The conflict involves different people, so someone can tell which one is theirs.

pairs.distinction: Caregiving is looking after a sick, disabled or aging person; parenting is raising your own kids.
pairs.reason: Most people would not call raising their kids caregiving, and the help available is different.

pairs.distinction: Caregiving names the cause; no time of my own can come from work, kids or anything else.
pairs.reason: Caregiving takes far more than time, so it stands as its own pain on People.
Being worn out raising kids is personal, while the cost of childcare is a shared problem, so each belongs on its own page with a link between them.

data.notes: Eighteen lists read. oecd.org was not fetched (403 in earlier runs), so OECD entries are the Housing, Safety and Environmental quality indicators as named in the framework key, with one TUAC passage. Eurostat: overcrowding, keep-warm and overburden from Statistics Explained 'Living conditions in Europe - housing' (2024); noise and pollution from the quality-of-life article (2023); the leaking roof/damp/rot figure from Trading Economics' mirror of Eurostat data (2024). Gallup Most Important Problem has no housing row; only Poverty/Hunger/Homelessness and Crime/Violence bear on home. Ipsos has no housing worry; its crime passage is the one country line the page gave. WHO burden lists name household air pollution (open-fire cooking), marked out of scope for U.S. readers. 'High indoor temperatures' is mapped broader to Heating: its alias 'Cold or hot home' suggests heat was meant, but the line names only heating; refine should decide whether to widen it. Living with parents: Pew finds housing costs are not associated with metro rates, so the line avoids naming a cause. Tap water overlaps Pollution (dirty-air) and Infrastructure from the home side. Two drafts (Repairs, Rental applications) come only from the founder pool and have no opened source. Wikidata QIDs from the wbsearchentities API (rate-limited, retried; not counted as searches). PDFs were read locally because the fetch tool could not parse them.
